ifNpcDead.resolution: If Willa Seaver is already dead, Ned Seaver has the private copy and hates it more, not less. He will not burn it, because she would not, and he asks Rowan Keel to give the contradiction to the student or to refuse. He will not become the explainer.

n_open.text: Willa's dead and this is still here, both sentences, shut and opened late. A student wants the clean one. I hate paperwork, Rowan Keel. I won't burn her page and I won't lecture him into being a better person. Give it or refuse it. Then I'm done being in this rented room. Norma can win or not. I just won't be the priest of the drawer.

choices.text: Give the student Willa's contradictory copy.
Refuse, and leave the copy in the survey room.

n_end_given_ned.text: Given. If he makes it content, I don't want to hear the content. Willa Seaver wanted the smear felt. I wanted the desk clear. You picked her, Rowan. Fine. I'm leaving the building. The flood page is his problem now, and I will not chase it to add a warning label. Warnings are more paperwork.

n_end_refused_ned.text: Refused. Norma gets the clean story, wherever she is. I won't call that a victory. I'll call it less paper in a backpack. Rowan Keel, don't you ask me to reopen the drawer for a better speech. Willa didn't burn it. I didn't burn it. The student leaves with the easy version. I can stand that better than a performance.

ifNpcDead.resolution: If Ned Seaver is already dead, Owen Perch will not caress the paperwork. Willa Seaver's copy is on the table. He tells Rowan Keel to give the contradiction or refuse it, and he will not stay to watch a student be improved.

n_open.text: Ned's dead, so you don't get his complaining, you get mine. Willa still thinks a stranger should feel the smear. Norma still wins if he doesn't. I refuse this desk as a life, Rowan Keel. I don't refuse your choice. Give the page or don't. Say it so I can go back to work that isn't a private copy of somebody's contradiction.

choices.text: Give the contradictory copy and let Owen leave.
Refuse the copy and send Owen out with an empty hand.

n_end_given_owen.text: Given. I hope the student is bored by it. Boredom would be safer than content. Willa Seaver gets her risk. I get to leave Middlebury's rented room. Don't you offer me a copy of my own, Rowan. I have practiced refusing keys, chairs, and pages. The flood's two sentences are not my craft. They're yours for the afternoon.

n_end_refused_owen.text: Refused. The clean story keeps its advantage. I won't pretend that's brave. Ned Seaver would have hated the meeting and agreed with the no. That's the only remark I have for him. The page stays in the drawer, Rowan Keel. Norma wins this round from the grave. I am not staying to argue with a dead woman's neatness.

endingImplications: Giving the contradictory copy may turn Ivo Perch's two sentences into something a stranger can pass around. Refusing it keeps the clean story in circulation and lets Norma's neatness win from the grave. Willa will not burn the page to escape the choice.

title: The Slate
summary: In 1966 Constance Daly has walked to the Waite house in Orwell for Cress Moss's slate. Joel, fourteen, wrote over the handwriting without knowing. Constance wants a penmanship lesson. Miriam Waite wants the slate back. Ada Smollet sends it to the school or keeps it at the house.
discovery: On the Orwell house step, Constance Daly waits with a teacher's certainty and Miriam Waite holds the slate against her skirt. Joel's writing is on top. Under it, where the cloth rubbed, Cress Moss's hand still shows. Ada is not invited in as if the house were glad.

steps.playerAction: Meet Constance Daly on the step of the Waite house and look at the slate Joel wrote over.
Choose whether the slate goes to the Orwell school or stays at the Quiet Household.
Say the choice so Miriam Waite and Constance Daly both hear it, and do not send the boy to carry it.

n_open.text: The hand underneath is beautiful. Children can learn from a beautiful hand. Joel wrote over it. He is fourteen and he did not know he was covering Cress Moss's last ordinary lines. If you tell me the slate is private, Ada Smollet, I will return it on this step. I will also think the house is hoarding a lesson. I can live with your opinion. Miriam already thinks I can live with too much.

choices.text: Let the slate go to the school as a penmanship lesson.
Keep the slate at the house and tell Constance it is private.

textVariants.text: Say the name before the slate moves, if you are going to say anything, Ada. An unspoken name is how a lesson steals a person. Miriam Waite will tell you not to make the boy say it. She is right about that. The name is Cress Moss. I am Constance Daly, and I walked here from the school because the hand is worth learning. The house can still refuse me.

n_mid_school.text: Take it, then. Joel does not get a speech and he does not get to undo the writing. Cress had a day that was ordinary. You are about to make it instructive, Constance. Ada Smollet, if you call this a kindness to the dead, I will correct you on this step. It is a loss I am allowing. The Quiet Household does not applaud its losses.

n_end_school.text: The school will use the hand, and I will say the name Cress Moss once, so it is not only pretty loops. I think the house is poorer for agreeing. I also think the children in Orwell are richer. Those can both be true, Miriam. I won't gloat on your step. Ada, you chose a lesson. I will try not to waste the hand you gave up.

n_mid_house.text: Private, then. I return it, as I said I would. I think the Quiet Household is hoarding a lesson, and I think the lines Joel wrote over Cress Moss are not a shrine. They are a boy's work on a used slate. Ada Smollet, you may keep your reasons. I have a class that will use a lesser example and will not be ruined. Miriam, your opinion of me is already priced in.

n_end_house.text: It stays. I don't need Constance Daly to approve, and I don't need you to comfort the boy. He wrote over Cress without knowing. The correction is that we stop passing her around Orwell. Ada, that is the whole thanks you are not getting. The slate goes back inside the door. The step is done being a school.

branches.summary: The slate goes to the Orwell school as a penmanship lesson, Constance Daly will say Cress Moss's name once, and Miriam Waite allows the loss without calling it kindness.
The slate stays at the Waite house, Constance Daly returns it and thinks the household is hoarding a lesson, and Miriam Waite does not offer thanks.
With Constance Daly dead, Miriam Waite still lets the slate go to the school and refuses both thanks and the boy's performance of regret.
Miriam Waite keeps Cress Moss's slate at the house after Constance Daly's death, and Ada Smollet is not thanked for agreeing.
The slate goes to the school from the step after Miriam Waite's death, Joel is not brought out to speak, and no one supplies the thanks she would have withheld.
Constance Daly leaves the slate at the house as a private thing, thinks the household is hoarding a lesson, and does not put Joel in the doorway.

rewards.detail: Cress Moss's slate, overwritten by a fourteen-year-old's hand, either carried to the Orwell school or kept in the Quiet Household.
Ada Smollet chose whether a beautiful hand was a lesson or a private ordinary thing, and did not make Joel speak for the dead lines.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Ada Smollet dies on the step before the slate moves. Miriam Waite keeps it in the house and does not thank Ellis, because there is no one left in the doorway worth thanking.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The slate is never decided. Miriam Waite keeps it at the Quiet Household, and she does not thank Ellis for a choice that was never finished on the step.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The slate is at the Orwell school or at the house, as chosen. Miriam Waite's lack of thanks, if she withheld it, stays withheld. The season does not add a gratitude she refused.

ifNpcDead.resolution: If Constance Daly is already dead, Miriam Waite still has to decide whether Cress Moss's slate leaves the house for the school or stays. She will not make Joel the spokesman. Ada Smollet's choice is the outside mouth she will accept.

n_open.text: Constance is dead. The school will send someone eventually, and they will be less honest than she was. Joel wrote over Cress Moss and he is not coming out to perform regret. Tell me the slate goes to Orwell's school, Ada Smollet, or tell me it stays. Do it on this step. I will not make a fourteen-year-old into the voice of a handwriting.

choices.text: Send the slate to the school even without Constance to carry it.
Keep the slate at the house with Constance gone.

n_end_school_miriam.text: Then it goes, and I will hate the wrapping. Cress Moss becomes a lesson without the woman who at least would have said her name on the step. Ada Smollet, walk it as far as the road. I won't thank you. Joel stays inside. The Quiet Household keeps the loss and not the slate. That is the arithmetic I agreed to.

n_end_house_miriam.text: It stays. The school can think we hoard. Constance Daly already would have thought that, and she would have returned it anyway if we called it private. I am returning it to the house. You don't get gratitude for agreeing with me, Ada Smollet. Joel does not come to the door. Cress's hand stays an ordinary thing.

ifNpcDead.resolution: If Miriam Waite is already dead, the slate is still at the Orwell house and Constance Daly is still on the step. Joel is fourteen and is not made to speak for the handwriting he covered. Ada Smollet decides whether the lesson leaves or the house keeps it.

n_open.text: Miriam is dead, and the slate is in the hall where she left it. I still want it for penmanship, Ada Smollet. I will return it if you tell me Cress Moss's hand is private, and I will think the house is hoarding a lesson. The boy is inside. Don't you put Joel in the doorway to settle this. He wrote over her without knowing. That is not a speech.

choices.text: Give Constance the slate for the Orwell school.
Keep the slate in the house and call Cress's hand private.

n_end_school_constance.text: Ada Smollet puts the slate in Constance Daly's hands on the step of the Waite house. Joel stays unseen and unasked. The overwritten lines and Cress Moss's hand go to the Orwell school together. There is no Miriam Waite in the doorway to withhold thanks, so the thanks simply do not happen. Constance says the name once and leaves.

n_end_house_constance.text: Private, then, and the keeper who would have agreed with you is dead. I return a thing I was never quite given. I think you are hoarding a lesson, Ada Smollet. Joel did not ask to be a memorial, and I did not ask him to be one. I can live with your opinion. I can walk back to the Orwell school without the slate.

endingImplications: If the slate goes to the school, children learn a beautiful hand and the house loses a private ordinary thing. If it stays, Constance Daly returns it and thinks the household is hoarding a lesson. Miriam can live with that opinion. She will not add thanks.

title: The Stopped Minute
summary: In 1980 Joel Waite is old enough to wind the hall clock past the minute Harold stopped, the minute before Ellis woke in Rennet. Winding kills a minute the house worships. Not winding means living in a stopped house. Miriam Waite tells Louis Pell not to help, only to witness.
discovery: The hall clock at the Waite house in Orwell stands at the old minute. Joel Waite has the key. Miriam Waite stands where she can see both the clock and Louis Pell's hands, and she has already forbidden help. Harold Waite is dead and is not a voice in the hall.

steps.playerAction: Stand in the hall where the stopped minute is visible and Joel Waite can see that your hands are empty.
Hear Miriam Waite forbid help and require Louis Pell to witness whatever her son does with the key.
Witness Joel wind the clock or witness the clock left stopped, without putting a hand on the case.

n_open.text: Joel is old enough to wind it. I am old enough to stop pretending my hand is the only honest one. Harold stopped this clock at the minute before you woke in Rennet, and Harold is dead. Don't help, Louis Pell. Witness. If Joel winds it, a worshipped minute dies. If he doesn't, he lives in a stopped house. I will not make the choice for him to keep my own hands clean.

choices.text: Witness Joel Waite wind the clock past the stopped minute.
Witness the choice to leave Harold's clock stopped.

textVariants.text: No. I see you lean toward the case, Louis. That want is a latch you do not get to finish. Joel Waite decides. You witness. Harold's minute is not your repair and not your gate. Hands off the glass. The Quiet Household has had enough people who cannot leave a thing half done. Today the half-done thing has a son.

n_mid_wound.text: If I wind it, I am killing a minute you all worship. I know. I have lived next to it since the year I was born. Move your hands where I can see them, Louis Pell. I want the witness and I don't want the help. Mother said her hand is not the only honest one. She can watch me prove it. Harold is dead. The minute doesn't get a vote.

n_end_wound.text: Wound. The house can tell the time that continued, which it did, for everyone who was not displaced that morning and not Harold. Louis, you witnessed. You didn't help. I won't thank you for obedience. I will remember that Joel Waite's hand was the one on the key. The worshipped minute is over. Orwell can have a ticking hall.

n_mid_left.text: Then say it, Joel, so the witness hears a sentence and not a mood. I am not touching the case. That was the promise I made to myself when I said my hand would not be the only honest one. Louis Pell, keep your hands where we can both see them. The minute before Rennet woke is still the minute on the face. It can stay if my son says stay.

n_end_left.text: It stays stopped. I am choosing the stopped house with my eyes open, not because Mother's hand is the only honest one. Louis, you saw me not wind it. Don't you come back and call that fate. Harold Waite is dead. I am not. The clock is a decision now, which is more than it was when it was only his habit. I can live in the minute. I just did.

branches.summary: Joel Waite winds the hall clock past Harold's stopped minute while Louis Pell only witnesses, and Miriam Waite does not pretend her hand was required.
Joel Waite leaves Harold's clock stopped on purpose, Louis Pell witnesses without helping, and the house keeps the minute before Rennet woke.
Miriam Waite winds the clock herself after Joel's death, hating that she is again the only hand, while Louis Pell only witnesses.
Miriam Waite leaves the clock stopped after Joel's death and will not use his absence as the courage to wind Harold's minute.
Joel Waite winds the clock after Miriam's death, keeps her rule that Louis Pell only witness, and ends the minute Harold stopped.
Joel Waite leaves the hall clock stopped of his own accord after Miriam Waite's death, and Louis Pell's hands stay off the case.

rewards.detail: Louis Pell knows the hall clock was stopped at the minute before Rennet Moss woke, and knows whether that minute was moved.
Louis Pell witnessed and did not help, which is the only stance Miriam Waite was willing to allow beside Harold's clock.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Louis Pell dies in the hall before the key turns or is refused. The clock stays stopped, because nobody would wind it over a body in the hall.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: No one winds the clock. It stays stopped, and the reason people repeat is the hard one: nobody would wind it over a body in the hall, or over a decision that never got said.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The clock is wound or it is not, as the Waite who held the key decided in front of a witness. A later season does not put Harold's minute back as if the hall had been empty of choice.

ifNpcDead.resolution: If Joel Waite is already dead, Miriam Waite is returned to the only honest hand, the role she refused. She will wind Harold's clock herself or leave it stopped, and Louis Pell still only witnesses. She will not pretend the son is in the hall.

n_open.text: Joel is dead. I said I would not be the only honest hand. Death doesn't negotiate with a sentence I liked. Harold's minute is still stopped, the minute before Rennet woke. I can wind it, Louis Pell, or I can leave this house stopped. You witness. You do not help. I will not make his absence pretty, and I will not ask the clock to be a memorial with better manners.

choices.text: Witness Miriam wind the clock because Joel cannot.
Witness Miriam leave the clock stopped.

n_end_wound_miriam.text: Wound, by the wrong person. The worshipped minute is dead. Louis Pell, you saw that I did it and that I didn't want to. Don't you write that Joel Waite would have agreed. He isn't in this hall to agree. Harold stopped it. I started it. The Quiet Household can tell ordinary time now, and I am angry at the ordinary.

n_end_left_miriam.text: Stopped, then. I live in Harold's minute because the son who could have ended it is dead, and I will not spend Joel Waite's death as my courage. You witnessed a refusal, Louis Pell. It is a poorer refusal than the one I wanted, which was his. The case stays untouched. That is the only honesty I have left in this hall.

ifNpcDead.resolution: If Miriam Waite is already dead, Joel Waite still has the key and no mother to forbid help. He tells Louis Pell to witness anyway, because that was her sentence, and he will wind the clock or leave it without a second hand on the case.

n_open.text: She said don't help, witness. She's dead, so the order has to come from me. I'll wind Harold's minute out of this house, Louis Pell, or I'll leave us stopped. Hands off the case. I want one witness who isn't a parent and isn't a speech. The Quiet Household can tick or not. It cannot have your fingers on the glass and call that my decision.

choices.text: Witness Joel wind the clock with no one to stop him.
Leave the clock stopped and say why, without Miriam there.

n_end_wound_joel.text: Done. The house can keep time like other houses in Orwell. I won't call it an insult to Harold Waite. I'll call it a decision I made while you watched and didn't help. That was her term, Louis. I kept the term. Mother isn't here to see the minute die. I saw it. The key worked. The worshipped stop is over.

n_end_left_joel.text: Stopped. Not because she was watching. Because I still think a worshipped minute is truer than a tidy hall, and I am willing to live in it. Louis Pell, you witnessed. Don't help it later when I'm out of the room. Harold Waite stopped it for a reason I didn't choose. I am choosing it now. That's different, and it's mine.

endingImplications: If Joel winds the clock, the house loses the minute it has treated as honest since 1952. If the clock stays stopped, he keeps living inside Harold's refusal. Louis Pell's part is witness, not a hand on the key. Either outcome is a household fact.

title: Christian's Meal
summary: The Quiet Household has cooked the Thursday Christian Dobbs wrote down for himself, and Chris's hands expect it. Eating comforts the body. Leaving the plate keeps the food as leftovers. Cooking it wrong on purpose tells the truth and is a little cruel.
discovery: You are in the Orwell kitchen because the plate is already on the table, not because anyone called you in from the road. Miriam Waite is failing and still standing at the stove. Joel Waite watches Chris's hands find the fork. The meal is hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the store bread.

steps.playerAction: Stand at the Quiet Household table and hear Christian's Thursday list read as groceries with a name, not as a rite.
Decide whether Chris's hands get the meal they expect, whether the plate stays full, or whether the food is ruined on purpose.
Say, in the kitchen, whether comfort was allowed, refused, or spoiled, and leave the fork where that decision puts it.

n_open.text: Christian wrote hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the store bread on the fridge paper, and that is what is on the table. Chris's hands keep finding the fork. It is groceries with a name on them. I am too tired to pretend it is more, and too stubborn to pretend it is less.

choices.text: Eat Christian's Thursday so the hands can stop looking for it.
Leave the plate where it is and do not feed the hands.
Cook it wrong on purpose so the body is not comforted.

textVariants.text: You will want to feed those hands and call the feeding a kindness, and you will want the kindness to count as accurate. Christian's list is hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the bread. Chris already believes the plate. If you spare him, say so. If you spare yourself, say that instead.

n_mid_eaten.text: The hands quit hunting once the peas were gone. That is the whole mercy and I am not going to sneer at a clean plate. Mother will not put the fork in a drawer and call it memory. It is a fork. You used it. The name was Christian and the food was food.

n_end_eaten.text: You ate what Christian would have eaten, and the body is quieter for it. I am not going to thank you, and I am not going to save the plate. Joel can wash it with the others. If comfort was the true thing, then it has already happened, and this house can be ordinary for one Thursday.

n_mid_refused.text: Then it stays until the peas go dull. Chris's hands can be disappointed without this kitchen turning disappointment into a rule. I cooked what the paper said because the paper was his. You do not have to finish another man's Thursday to prove you saw his name.

n_end_refused.text: I'll put it in the icebox, not on a shelf with a card under it. A plate you refused is leftovers, and leftovers are allowed to be thrown out on Friday. Mother can hate the waste. I can live with waste. I cannot live with a hamburger becoming a household job.

n_mid_cooked_wrong.text: You put sugar on the peas and you did it where we could both see you. That is not a mistake and the hands know it, which is the point you wanted. The point is mean. It is also plain. Christian's list did not ask for a lesson, and you gave the body a bad plate instead of a lullaby.

n_end_cooked_wrong.text: I understand why you spoiled it. A correct meal would have told Chris's hands they were still in Christian's Thursday, and you would not tell that lie. I do not admire the cruelty. Take the fork out of those hands. The groceries have done their honest work, and the honest work was to fail.

branches.summary: Ellis eats Christian Dobbs's meal. The body is comforted and the plate goes into the wash with the others.
Ellis leaves Christian's plate. The food stays leftovers, and the hands do not get the comfort they expected.
Ellis cooks the meal wrong on purpose. The body is not comforted, and the household sees that the failure was chosen.
With Miriam dead, Joel serves the meal and Ellis eats it. The plate is washed with the ordinary dishes.
With Miriam dead, Ellis still refuses the meal. Joel treats it as leftovers and will not start a new practice.
With Miriam dead, Ellis still ruins the meal on purpose. Joel sees the meanness and does not dress it up.
With Joel dead, Eden names the meal as groceries and Ellis eats it. Miriam does not turn the plate into a keepsake.
With Joel dead, Ellis leaves the plate. Eden stores it as leftovers and says the name once without a shelf.
With Joel dead, Ellis cooks the meal wrong. Eden lets the cruelty stay visible and then throws the food out.

rewards.detail: The household knows whether Ellis would comfort Chris's hands with Christian's own groceries.
Christian's Thursday was hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the store bread, and the hands expected it.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Joel eats the hamburger, the peas, and the heel of bread himself at the kitchen table so the plate cannot be saved as a shrine. Ellis dies before the choice, and leftovers are easier to throw out than a story with a name on it.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The era turns with the plate undecided. Christian's list stays on the fridge, Chris's hands stay restless, and nobody writes down whether the body was allowed a comfort or refused one.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The Thursday is over. The next wearing does not inherit a reheated argument about Christian Dobbs's plate, only the fact that the groceries were faced in the Orwell kitchen while Miriam was still alive.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Miriam is gone, so Joel cooks from the fridge paper himself and will not let Christian's list become a speech. He still offers the same three uses of the food, and he washes or ruins the plate without asking the house for a blessing.

n_open.text: Mother is not here to stand at the stove and look stern about it. Christian's paper still says hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the bread. I can feed Chris's hands, leave the plate, or ruin it on purpose so nobody calls leftovers a rite. Pick before it cools into a story.

choices.text: Eat the Thursday Joel cooked from the paper.
Leave Joel's plate in the icebox untouched.
Spoil the peas on purpose and let Joel see it.

n_end_eaten_joel.text: All right. The hands stopped. I am washing this with the breakfast bowls and I am not keeping the recipe. Mother would have hated the waste of a speech more than the waste of peas. You ate. Christian's name got said once. That is the end of the groceries.

n_end_refused_joel.text: Then the icebox gets it, and Friday gets the trash. I will not put a card under it because Mother is dead and I am not starting a new job in her place. The hands can be unhappy. Unhappy is not the same as a household rule about forks.

n_end_wrong_joel.text: Sugar on the peas, in front of me. Fine. You wanted the hands to know they were not being tucked in. They know. I think it is a mean way to be honest and I will still eat the ruined plate myself later so it does not sit here looking like a moral. Not tonight. Tonight you said the thing.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Joel is gone, so Eden handles the plate without mocking the list he resented. Miriam may still be in the house, but the decision is Eden's to say in a whole sentence: eat, leave, or spoil, and then get on with the dishes.

n_open.text: Joel is not here to resent the portion, and I am not going to do his resentment for him. Christian's list is still hamburger, canned peas, and the heel of the bread. Portion is groceries. I can give it to the hands, leave it, or cook it wrong. I will not make fun of the paper while I do it.

choices.text: Eat, and let Eden clear the plate with the rest.
Leave the food and let Eden call it leftovers.
Ruin the meal on purpose and let Eden watch.

n_end_eaten_eden.text: Eden said portion and she was right. You ate the portion. My hands are not what they were, so she will wash, and I will not tell her to dry it as if Christian were still owed a towel. The body is quieter. That was the only use of the peas.

n_end_refused_eden.text: Then I put it away as leftovers and I say Christian's name once so we do not pretend we forgot who wrote the list. The hands do not get the comfort. I can live with that if we do not build a shelf for the refusal. Mother can be angry at the waste. Waste is cheaper than a rite.

n_end_wrong_eden.text: You spoiled good food so the hands would not be lied to. I see it and I am not going to laugh, and I am not going to scold you into cooking it over. Honest and mean can sit in the same bowl. I'll dump it when you're done looking at it. The list can stay on the fridge as a list.

endingImplications: The Quiet Household either let a living body be comforted by a dead man's ordinary meal, left the food as leftovers, or spoiled it on purpose. None of those outcomes is a ceremony. The fork is just a fork afterward, and Christian's name stays attached to a Thursday rather than to a shrine.

title: Today's Coat
summary: A coat turns in the eddy under the Vergennes falls. Osier Rouleau wants it to be the 1938 loss so he already knows the procedure. Marie Rouleau says the wool is wet from this week and belongs to somebody who is missing it today.
discovery: You are on the basin rock because the falls are loud and the coat is already caught in the eddy. Osier has his old book open to a year he trusts. Marie is on the same rock with flour still on her cuff, and she is not letting him write the year down yet.

steps.playerAction: Look at the coat in the eddy and hear Osier name 1938 while Marie names this week, without leaving the basin.
Choose whether to shout for today's help from where you stand, or to let Osier file the coat under the old loss.
Stay on the rock until the coat is either claimed as this week's or written into the procedure Osier already knows.

n_open.text: Coat in the eddy, dark wool, one button gone. I have done this. Nineteen thirty-eight, we logged it, we named the year, we knew which hook to use. If it is that loss again, I know the work. Don't make me invent a new work while the water is this loud.

choices.text: Shout for the day shift at the rail and call this coat this week's.
Let Osier enter the coat as the 1938 loss and use the old procedure.

textVariants.text: You hate an unfinished count and I can see it in the way you look at the book. The coat is in the eddy now, this week, wet through. I would love to close it under 1938 because a closed year is a job I can finish. Marie says a living person is missing the wool. Pick the job you can stand to leave open.

n_mid_today.text: You shouted for the day shift and you did not climb off the rock to go find a clerk. I heard the names you used. Upper rail, night-kitchen door, whoever is short a work coat since Monday. That is a living errand done with your mouth. The wool is still in the eddy and it is not a relic.

n_end_today.text: All right. I shut the old page. The coat is today's, and the help you shouted for can claim it when they get to the basin edge. I do not get my procedure. Marie gets a wet coat with a chance of an owner. I will write the day of the week and nothing else, and I will hate how thin that looks.

n_mid_old_wound.text: Then I do the thing I know. Year first, then the hook, then the note that the basin has taken this kind of wool before. My hand is steady when the year is one I have already survived. You are giving me that steadiness. Marie is looking at me as if steadiness were a theft.

n_end_old_wound.text: You let him write 1938 on a coat that was dry on somebody this morning. The procedure will be beautiful and the person missing the wool will not be in it. I am staying on this rock. I will not run your errand either. I will remember that you chose a year you could finish over a week you could not.

branches.summary: Ellis treats the coat as this week's loss and shouts for the day shift without leaving the basin. Osier closes the 1938 page.
Ellis forces the coat into the 1938 story. Osier gets his procedure, and the person missing it this week is left out of the book.
With Osier dead, Marie and Ellis treat the coat as this week's and shout for the day shift from the basin.
With Osier dead, Marie still files the coat as 1938 because Ellis asks her to finish his procedure.
With Marie dead, Osier still abandons 1938 and shouts for this week's owner from the basin.
With Marie dead, Osier files the coat under 1938 and gets the procedure he wanted.

rewards.detail: The basin coat was wet from this week, whatever year Osier needed it to be.
Ellis either shouted for a living owner from the rock or gave Osier the 1938 procedure.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Marie hangs the coat on the basin nail where a living person can claim it, and she will not let Osier name the year. Ellis's shout dies with Ellis. The wool drips on the rock and the old page stays shut because she puts her hand on it.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The era moves on with the coat still unclaimed and the year unwritten. The falls keep the wool moving in the eddy, and neither the day shift nor the 1938 page is ever made to own it.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The basin keeps the choice. Either a this-week shout went up from the rock, or the old procedure took the coat, and the next wearing does not get to reopen the wool as if nobody had spoken.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Osier is dead, so Marie has the book and will not let a dead man's favorite year swallow a coat that is wet this week. She still forces Ellis to choose between a shout for the living and a page that knows its procedure.

n_open.text: Osier is dead and his book is on the rock with the page he loved already marked. The coat in the eddy is wet from this week. I can shout for the day shift with you, or I can write the year he would have written. I will not pretend those are the same kindness. Say which one you will stand for.

choices.text: Shout for the day shift and keep 1938 off the page.
Tell Marie to enter the coat under 1938 anyway.

n_end_today_marie.text: Then I shout with you, from here, for the upper rail and the night-kitchen door. The coat stays today's. I will not walk it up to a desk. When the day shift comes to the edge they can claim the wool, and Osier's page can stay a page. I am not giving his death the button off this coat.

n_end_old_marie.text: Then I write the year he wanted, and I hate my hand while it moves. The procedure gets finished. The person who wore this on Monday does not. You asked a dead man's habit to do the work of looking. I will hang the coat after, but the book will already have lied about when it got wet.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Marie is dead, so Osier is alone with the eddy and the temptation of a year he understands. He will still take a shouted name for this week if Ellis gives him one, and he will not invent Marie's objection in a softer voice.

n_open.text: Marie is dead and the coat does not care. It is in the eddy, dark wool, one button gone. I want it to be 1938 because I know that page. She would have said it was wet this week. She is not here to say it. You say whether I shout for the day shift or whether I finish the old job.

choices.text: Make Osier shout for the day shift and write this week.
Let Osier use the 1938 procedure with no one to stop him.

n_end_today_osier.text: I shouted. Upper rail, day shift, a coat short since Monday. I did not leave the rock and I did not open 1938. The page looks thin. Marie would have liked it thin. I will not like it. The wool can be claimed by somebody living, which is the trouble she would have insisted on.

n_end_old_osier.text: Then the year goes in, and the hook, and the note. I know this work and the knowing is a relief I am ashamed of, because she is dead and cannot slap the book. The coat becomes the old loss. If a living person is missing it, they will have to argue with a page that has already decided.

endingImplications: Vergennes either treats the eddy coat as a loss from this week, with help shouted from the basin, or files it under 1938 so Osier can follow a procedure he already trusts. A living owner's chance and an old year's comfort do not both fit on the same line.

title: The Sugarhouse Acres
summary: The sugarhouse ledger and the county map do not show the same maple acres. Fixing the number makes the Harrow homestead pay what it owes, and the bill will hurt. Leaving the wrong acres keeps a kind tax and a false map. Nell talks about the debt, not a verdict.
discovery: The ledger is already open on the bench above the arch, and the county map is folded beside it with a pencil holding the crease. You are in the sugarhouse because the boil is going and Nell Harrow has both numbers in front of her. Nobody has to walk to a clerk for the argument to be real.

steps.playerAction: Read the sugarhouse ledger against the county map while the boil is going, both of them already on the bench.
Choose whether the homestead will pay the acres it owes or keep the kind, smaller number.
Tell Nell which figure she is willing to be resented for, and leave the ledger as that choice makes it.

n_open.text: The sugarhouse book says forty-one acres in the maples. The county map says sixty-two. The difference is a kindness with a number on it. Fix it and we pay. Leave it and I read a lie every boil. I am not asking the row for a verdict. I am asking what we are willing to owe.

choices.text: Correct the ledger to the map and let the homestead pay.
Leave the wrong acres so the kind tax stays in place.

textVariants.text: You like a page that tells the truth, and you also flinch when the truth sends a bill to a house you answer for. Forty-one in the ledger, sixty-two on the map. The kind number is the false one. If you spare us the tax, say you are sparing us. Don't call the forty-one a measurement.

n_mid_fixed.text: Then I strike forty-one and I write sixty-two, and I initial it so the clerk cannot pretend the sugarhouse disagreed with itself. The boil does not care. The tax will. Mother will hear the number and she will not call it poetry. Good. I don't want poetry in a ledger.

n_end_fixed.text: It's fixed. We will pay what the maples actually cover, and we will feel it in a year when the syrup price is ordinary. Louis, if that is the name your mouth is using today, you don't get to comfort me about it. The row owed taxes. It did not owe us a softer acre.

n_mid_left.text: Then forty-one stays, and I do not initial a correction I am refusing to make. The map can be right in the drawer and wrong in the bill. That is a common arrangement in this county. I want you to hear me not dressing it up. I am choosing the cheaper lie because the cheaper lie pays for sugar wood.

n_end_left.text: The book stays wrong. If anyone calls it mercy, they can do it outside this sugarhouse. I won't. We keep the kind tax and we keep a false map, and I will see both numbers every time I boil. That is the cost of not paying. It is not a verdict. It is an invoice we decided not to receive.

branches.summary: Nell corrects the sugarhouse acres to the county map. The homestead will pay the harder, true bill.
Nell leaves the ledger acres wrong. The tax stays kind, the map stays false, and she will not call that mercy.
With Nell dead, Maeve corrects the acres. The homestead pays, and she refuses to turn the bill into a speech.
With Nell dead, Maeve leaves the wrong acres. She keeps the kind tax and will not call the lie a kindness out loud.

rewards.detail: The sugarhouse ledger either matches the county map or keeps the kind, wrong acreage on purpose.
The book said forty-one maple acres and the county map said sixty-two, and the gap was a tax.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: The ledger stays wrong, forty-one where the map says sixty-two, and Nell does not call it mercy out loud. Ellis dies before the strike-through. She closes the book, keeps the kind tax, and refuses the softer word.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The era advances with both numbers still sitting on the bench in memory if not in fact. No one has initialed a correction, and the homestead has not admitted whether it meant to keep the kindness.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The sugarhouse number is settled for this boil and the ones after it. Either the bill goes up because the acres were fixed, or the false ledger remains as a choice Nell will not prettify.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Nell is dead, so Maeve stands at the arch with her daughter's ledger and will not pretend the acreage is a family riddle. She can fix the tax or leave the kind number, and she will not call either choice a blessing on the row.

n_open.text: Nell is dead. Her book says forty-one. The map says sixty-two. She would have talked taxes until the room behaved. I talk like the row has been lied about. I can still fix the number or leave the kindness. Don't ask me to sound like her. Choose the bill.

choices.text: Have Maeve strike the kind acres and pay the true ones.
Tell Maeve to leave the ledger's forty-one acres in place.

n_end_fixed_maeve.text: Sixty-two. I wrote it. The homestead will pay and the payment will hurt, which is how I know the number was late and not holy. Nell can be dead and still be right about the tax. I will not add a speech. The arch can finish the boil.

n_end_left_maeve.text: Then the lie stays, and I will not call it mercy. Nell wouldn't have either. I am keeping a kind tax because the year is already expensive, and I am telling you that plainly. The map is in the drawer. Anyone who wants the truth can unfold it and then explain the money.

endingImplications: The Harrow homestead either starts paying tax on the maple acres the county map already knew, or it keeps a kinder bill and a book Nell can see is false. The row is not forgiven or condemned. It is priced.

title: June's Wood
summary: Kit Downing is selling scion wood from June Harrow's tree in the exchange yard. June would have given the sticks away. Maeve would keep them until they rotted into a principle. Kit is not gloating. He thinks wood should travel, and the sale can be stopped, paid for with the truth, or allowed.
discovery: The sticks are already on a crate behind the feed store, mud on the twine, a paper tag in Kit's hand. You are in the Saturday yard because that is where the wood is. Ada's shoes are in the same mud. Nothing has to be carried anywhere for the sale to be real.

steps.playerAction: Hear Kit say, in the exchange yard, that the sticks are June Harrow's scion wood and that he means to sell them cheap.
Choose whether to expose the sale here, to speak the orchard stake truth as the price of stopping it, or to let the wood travel.
Finish the talk before the sticks leave the crate or go back into the sack, with the yard still the whole scene.

n_open.text: June would have given this wood away over a fence and been done. Maeve will keep it until it rots into a principle with her name on the rot. I am selling it cheap so it becomes a tree in somebody else's ground. Call that a theft if you need a short word. I need a longer one.

choices.text: Say in the yard whose tree this wood was cut from.
Trade the truth about the orchard stake, spoken here, to stop the sale.
Let Kit sell the wood and let it leave the yard.

textVariants.text: You get restless when a true thing is sitting unspoken next to a price. These sticks are June's. The tag does not say her name. I will sell them unless you say something in this yard that is heavier than the tag. I am not daring you. I am telling you the wood is about to move.

n_mid_exposed.text: You said June Harrow's name loud enough for the next crate to hear, and you said the sticks were not mine to price. The man who was reaching for his wallet put his hand back in his coat. That is as stopped as a yard sale gets. Nobody is going to write a notice. They just won't buy.

n_end_exposed.text: The sale is done here. I still think a tree in another dooryard would have been a better monument than a sack in Maeve's patience, but I am not going to hawk June's wood after you made the yard look at me. Take the sticks or leave them. I am not wrapping them for a stranger now.

n_mid_traded.text: Ivo Perch moved the iron stake. The south block is Harrow silt, not county timber. I am saying that in this yard as the price of the sticks staying unsold. You do not get June's wood and the secret both. The mud can hear it. I am not walking it up to a different office to make it cleaner.

n_end_traded.text: Then I am not selling. The sticks go back in the sack. I wanted them to become a tree somewhere else, and you paid me a sentence about the stake instead. I am taking the sentence. Don't expect me to look holy. Maeve can still rot the wood into a principle if she gets the sack back. That is her trouble now, not mine.

n_mid_travel.text: Then I take the man's money and I give him two bundles, and I tell him to graft them where they will get sun and not a speech. June liked a graft that was allowed to fail in public. A tree in another town is public enough. You are letting it happen. I notice you not making a scene, and I am grateful without performing it.

n_end_travel.text: The wood is traveling. I sold it as itself, not as a relic, and the buyer knows it came off a Harrow tree because I said so when you didn't stop me. Maeve will call this a loss of principle. I call it a tree that might take. If it fails, it fails somewhere the row does not have to watch.

branches.summary: Ellis exposes the sale in the yard. Kit's buyers step back, and June's scion wood does not travel from this Saturday.
Ellis speaks the orchard stake truth in the yard as the price of stopping Kit's sale. The wood does not travel, and the stake is no longer hidden.
Ellis lets June's scion wood travel. Kit sells it cheap so it can become a tree off the Harrow row.
With Kit dead, Nell exposes the wood as June's and stops the sale in the yard.
With Kit dead, Ellis still speaks the stake truth in the yard. Nell stops the sale and keeps the wood.
With Kit dead, Nell lets the scion wood travel and says June's name without stopping the sale.

rewards.detail: A stick of June's scion wood either stays in the sack, goes back to the row, or leaves in a buyer's hand as proof of the yard's choice.
Ellis either exposed the sale, paid for stopping it with the stake truth, or let the wood travel.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Kit sells two sticks and keeps the rest in his pocket. Ellis dies before the yard can be made to look. The buyer gets a little wood. The sack is not a principle and not a gift. It is a pocket.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The Saturday ends with the sticks still on the crate and no one having said June's name, the stake, or a price that stuck. The wood is neither stopped nor truly sold. It is only waiting on the next hand.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The yard has already done the thing. June's wood was exposed, bought off with the truth about the stake, or allowed to travel, and a later season does not get to pretend the crate was never there.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Kit is dead, so Nell, twenty and already tired of principles, stands at his crate with the sticks. She can expose them, take the stake truth as a reason to hold them, or let the next buyer carry them off. She talks like a tax, not like a eulogy.

n_open.text: Kit is dead. His sticks are still on the crate and the man beside me will buy them if nobody speaks. Mother would keep them until they rot. June would have given them away. I am twenty. I want a result I can explain without a poem. Tell me which trouble you want in this mud.

choices.text: Have Nell say June's name and stop the sale here.
Speak the stake truth here and have Nell hold the wood.
Tell Nell to let the next buyer take the sticks.

n_end_exposed_nell.text: June Harrow. These are her sticks and they are not for sale this Saturday. I said it loud. The man's wallet stayed in his coat. I will take the sack back to the row and I will not promise Mother a principle. I promise her the wood is still wood. That is the tax I can stand.

n_end_traded_nell.text: I heard you. Ivo moved the stake. The south block is our silt, not county timber. You said it in the yard, so the price is paid and I am not selling. The sticks go home in the sack. I don't know yet if that makes me Mother. I know it stops a sale. Don't ask me to look grateful for a secret.

n_end_travel_nell.text: Then they travel. I took his money and I told him the tree's name because I am not a sneak, only a person letting wood leave. Mother will hate the receipt. June might have hated the receipt too and still wanted the graft to happen somewhere. I can live with being hated for a tree.

endingImplications: June Harrow's scion wood either stops in the exchange yard because the sale was named, stops because Ellis spoke the stake truth as a price, or leaves to become a tree somewhere else. Maeve's principle and June's giving cannot both be obeyed.

title: The Cows' Path
summary: Carl Abbott's cows use a path across the Harrow intervale because the flood moved the fence and his family kept walking. Asa is thirty-seven and wants the grass decided without a legend. Possession is not pretty, and it is how pastures work.
discovery: The cows are already on the intervale grass, and the fence that should have stopped them is lying where the high water left it. You are at the south block because Asa Harrow and Carl Abbott are both looking at the same hoof prints. The path is the argument. The paper that would describe it is not required for the grass to be decided.

steps.playerAction: Walk the hoof-cut path only as far as the broken fence and hear how long the Abbotts have been using it.
Choose whether the path stays with Asa and the cows are turned, or whether the cows keep the walking they already do.
Say the decision where both men can hear it, and leave the fence for the season it was given.

n_open.text: The fence went with the high water. Carl's family kept walking the cows across our intervale because the grass was here and the wire wasn't. He is honest about it. Possession is how pastures work and it is not pretty. I am thirty-seven. I want the grass decided, not inherited as a mood.

choices.text: Leave the path with Asa and turn Carl's cows back.
Leave the path under Carl's cows and let them keep walking.

textVariants.text: You don't like arguing with where water put a fence, and you also don't like correcting a habit that has been feeding somebody's cows. The wire is down. The path is worn. If you spare Carl a hard sentence, the grass stays his by use. If you spare me a false neighborliness, the cows get turned. Water already voted. You are the one left.

n_mid_asa_path.text: Then I turn them. Not with a speech and not with a shove worth telling about. I walk the lead cow back to where the wire used to hold and the others follow because they are cows. I have been using your grass since the flood. You are taking the use back. I understand it. I don't have to enjoy it.

n_end_asa_path.text: The path stays ours and the cows are off it. I will mend what I can before the next rain and I will not tell a story about victory at supper. Carl was not a thief. He was a man whose animals kept eating. Chris, if the hands fixing that fence are yours, don't make them heroic. Wire is wire.

n_mid_carl_path.text: Then they keep the path. I won't pretend the flood signed a paper. I will say we walked it every season the wire was down, and walking is the right I actually have. Asa can hate that and still be my neighbor. I would rather he hate a true use than like a fence I have not put back.

n_end_carl_path.text: The cows stay. I am not going to call it generosity. I am calling it the pasture as it is being used, which is Carl's sentence and also the ground. Possession isn't pretty. I will live beside it. If I change my mind I will change the wire, not the story, and I will say so before hay.

branches.summary: The intervale path stays with Asa. Carl turns the cows back, and the use since the flood is ended without a speech.
The path stays with Carl's cows. Asa accepts the use without calling it a gift, and the fence is not made into a legend.
With Asa dead, Nell takes the path back. Carl turns the cows and does not pretend use was a deed.
With Asa dead, Nell leaves the path to Carl's cows and refuses to call that a memorial gift.
With Carl dead, Nina turns the cows. Asa keeps the path and treats the fence repair as work.
With Carl dead, Nina keeps the cows on the path. The use continues without being called a victory.

rewards.detail: Ellis stood where the flood left the fence and chose whose feet the intervale path belongs under.
Either the Harrows have the path back or Carl's cows may keep walking it, and the other house knows which.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: The cows keep walking, and Asa fixes the fence in the spring without a speech. Ellis dies before the path is given to either name. The wire goes back up later as work, not as a verdict delivered in the orchard.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The season ends with the fence still down and the cows still on the grass. No one has said whether the walking is a right or a habit that can be ended, and the intervale stays undecided under their hooves.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The path has an owner in practice. Either Asa took it back and the cows were turned, or Carl's use was left in place, and the next year does not get to pretend the flood still needs a conversation.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Asa is dead, so Nell stands on the intervale she thought she had handed on. She will turn the cows or leave them, and she will not let Carl's honesty become a eulogy for her son. The grass still needs a sentence.

n_open.text: Asa is dead and the cows did not notice. Carl is still walking them where the flood laid our fence down. I can turn them in my son's place or I can leave the use where it is. I will not call either choice a memorial. Tell me who has the path before I get too old to mean it.

choices.text: Have Nell turn the cows and keep the path Harrow.
Tell Nell to leave the walking cows where they are.

n_end_asa_nell.text: Nell said turn, so I turn them. Asa isn't here to watch me do it politely, and I will do it politely anyway because the cows shouldn't pay for a death. The path is Harrow again. I had the use of it. Use is not a deed. I know the difference. I don't have to like meeting it.

n_end_carl_nell.text: Then Carl's cows keep it. I am not donating a path in Asa's name. I am refusing to move animals the flood already moved a fence for, and I am saying that without a ribbon on it. If the wire goes up later it will be a new decision. This one is: they walk.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Carl is dead, so Nina answers for the cows without wanting the family to remain a boundary dispute. Asa is still on the grass. Between them the path can be taken back or left under the herd, and the hours of explaining it will belong to the living.

n_open.text: My father is dead and the cows still know the path. I mow what I'm given and I explain the rest at town meeting if you reopen it. Asa wants the grass decided. I want us to stop being a fence with opinions. Turn them or leave them, and bring the hours the choice will cost.

choices.text: Turn the cows with Nina and give the path back to Asa.
Let Nina's cows keep the path they already walk.

n_end_asa_nina.text: Nina walked them back and did not make me a speech about her father. The path is ours again. I will fix the fence in the spring as work, not as a triumph over a dead neighbor. The flood moved the wire. We moved the cows. I can tell those apart.

n_end_carl_nina.text: Then we keep walking them. I won't call it my father's victory. I'll call it the way the herd already goes, and I will say that at town meeting if someone with a form asks. Asa can put the wire up when he means a new thing. Today the hooves stay.

endingImplications: The Harrow intervale path either returns to Asa, with Carl's cows turned back to the old fence line, or stays under the Abbotts' use because they kept walking after the flood. The pasture is decided by that sentence and not by a prettier story about water.

title: Peter's Other Shore
summary: Irene Voss has come only as far as the Vermont landing to ask whether Peter Voss can be named where his other people stand. Lena has to decide if the dead belong to the landing that watched the ice, or if the name can be released in a sentence toward the other shore.
discovery: Irene is already on the Vermont side of Chimney Point with her coat buttoned and no bag packed for a crossing. Lena has the landing log on the rail. Cal is four years dead and not in this talk. The question is a sentence about Peter, and the lake stays where it is.

steps.playerAction: Hear Irene ask, on the Vermont landing only, whether Peter can be named among his other people.
Decide with Lena whether the log keeps Peter as this shore's dead or releases his name in a sentence.
Speak the decision at the rail so the log can hold it, without anyone leaving the landing to perform it.

n_open.text: I didn't come to take your bridge and I didn't come to be walked across the lake. I came to ask whether Peter can be named where his other people stand. You can refuse. Do it in a whole sentence. I have a memorial on the other shore and a cousin who will not let a blank become a kindness.

choices.text: Keep Peter as the landing's dead and say so in a whole sentence.
Release Peter's name toward the other shore, in a sentence, from here.

textVariants.text: You keep two copies when one record feels like a loss, and I can see you wanting Peter written here and also over there. Lena will not love a double entry. I am asking for a release, not a second plaque. If the name is going to be said among his other people, somebody on this landing has to allow the sentence.

n_mid_landing.text: Then he stays in this log. My grandfather went through the ice on the Vermont side, and the landing watched it, and the watching is not nothing. Irene can be disappointed in a complete way. I will not smudge the line to make two shores feel fair. Fair is not a column I have.

n_end_landing.text: All right. You refused in a whole sentence, which is what I asked, and I am not going to pretend it was a small refusal. Peter remains yours in the book. I will go home by the road I came, still on this side until the road takes me, and I will tell them the landing kept him. I won't invent a warmer answer.

n_mid_release.text: Then I say it here, and I do not get in a car. Peter Voss may be named where his other people stand. This landing watched him die and does not own the only mouth that can say him. I am writing that beside his line so the log is not blank and not a locked door. Irene, that is the release. It is not a trip.

n_end_release.text: I heard the sentence. I am not asking you to come with me, and I am not asking the bridge to do a ceremony. The name can be said on the other shore because you allowed it from this rail. I will still call this the place that watched. I just won't call it the only place allowed to speak.

branches.summary: Peter stays the landing's dead. Irene's request is refused in a full sentence, and nobody crosses the lake to soften it.
Lena releases Peter's name in a sentence from the Vermont landing. The other shore may say him, and no one makes a trip of it.
With Irene dead, Lena still keeps Peter as the landing's dead and says the refusal without an audience.
With Irene dead, Lena releases Peter's name in the log anyway, from the Vermont rail, and does not travel.
With Lena dead, Noah keeps Peter in the landing log. Irene accepts the refusal without asking him to cross.
With Lena dead, Noah releases Peter's name from the Vermont landing in a plain sentence and does not make a trip of it.

rewards.detail: The landing log either keeps Peter as this shore's dead or notes that his name was released toward the other memorial.
Ellis stood at Chimney Point while Lena refused Irene or gave the name away in a sentence.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Lena keeps Peter's name in the landing log because a blank line frightens her more than Irene's disappointment. Ellis dies before a release can be said. Irene gets a whole sentence of refusal and the road home, not a crossing.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: Irene leaves without an answer she can repeat, and the log stays as Cal left it. Peter is neither released nor freshly claimed. The landing simply has not decided whether a state line owns a dead man.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The rail has a sentence in it now. Peter is either the landing's dead on purpose, or his name has been released toward the other shore without anyone leaving Vermont to prove it.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Irene is dead, so the request arrives as a letter Lena will not treat as poetry and as a decision she still has to make. She can keep Peter in the landing log or release the name without an audience from the other shore.

n_open.text: Irene is dead. Her question is not. She wanted Peter named where his other people stand, and she wanted the refusal, if I refused, to be a whole sentence. I can keep him as the landing's dead or I can release the name from this rail. I will not make the lake do the work.

choices.text: Keep Peter in the landing log and let Lena say the refusal.
Have Lena release the name from the rail with Irene gone.

n_end_landing_lena.text: He stays. I am sorry she is dead and I am not sorry enough to blank the line. The landing watched the ice. That is the claim. If her people say him anyway, they will be speaking over a book that did not release him. I can live with being the disappointing cousin in a sentence she asked for.

n_end_release_lena.text: Peter Voss may be named where his other people stand. I am writing that, and I am not traveling to watch them do it. Irene is dead so she does not get to hear me. The log still hears me. A blank would have frightened me more than giving the name away. This is not a blank. This is a release.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Lena is dead, so Noah has the log and Irene still has the question. He will not poeticize his mother's book. He can keep Peter as the landing's dead or release the name in one plain sentence from the Vermont side.

n_open.text: My mother is dead and the log is mine for this hour. Irene wants Peter said where his other people stand. I pump gas and I keep pages. I don't have a column for who owns a grandfather. Keep him here or release the name. Do it in words I can write without a poem.

choices.text: Tell Noah to keep Peter in the landing's dead.
Have Noah release Peter's name in one sentence from the rail.

n_end_landing_noah.text: Then the boy wrote it the way his mother would have, only shorter. Peter stays the landing's. I asked for a whole sentence and I got one. I am not going to punish a young man for inheriting a shore. I will tell the other people the book held. That is the disappointment, complete.

n_end_release_noah.text: I wrote it. Peter can be named on the other shore. I did not make it pretty and I am not driving anybody anywhere. The landing still watched the ice. Watching is not ownership. Irene can take the sentence. The log has it too, so we are not blank, which would have scared my mother worse than generosity.

endingImplications: Peter Voss is either kept as the Chimney Point dead, because the Vermont landing watched the ice, or his name is released in one sentence so his other people may say it. The lake is not crossed. The log is.

title: One Foot of Dooryard
summary: A corner post sits one foot inside the only flat place Alma Gray has for a chair, in Goshen. Moving it makes the line true and the dooryard cruel. Leaving it keeps the chair and makes the map a kindness that is also false. Ned hates both speeches and still wants one.
discovery: The post is already in the dooryard, and the chair is already beside it because that is the only level ground. You are in Goshen because Alma lives here and Ned walked up with the measurement. There is no crowd. There is one foot, one chair, and two ways to be wrong.

steps.playerAction: Stand in Alma Gray's dooryard and see the one foot between the corner post and a true line.
Choose whether the post moves, and the chair goes to the slope, or the post stays and the map stays kind.
Say the choice so Ned has the speech he hates and Alma has a place to sit or a reason to resent you.

n_open.text: One foot. The post is in the only flat I have for a chair. Move it if the line is true and I will sit on the slope, and I will not forgive you out loud. Leave it if you want me comfortable and the map wrong. I have lived with worse wrongness. I would like the chair.

choices.text: Move the post the one foot and let the chair lose its flat.
Leave the post and let Alma keep the only flat chair.

textVariants.text: You want the post to tell the truth, and you also hate to take a chair from an old woman for the sake of a foot. Ned is waiting to hate whichever speech you pick. Alma has already said she would like to sit. If you spare her, the map stays false. If you spare the record, she sits on the slope. Don't call either one gentle.

n_mid_moved.text: Then we move it. I hate the speech where a chair is a crime against a measurement, and I am making that speech anyway because you picked it. One foot. The line gets true. Alma's flat place gets smaller. I will not add a proverb about Goshen. The post comes out of the ground and goes where the number says.

n_end_moved.text: It's moved. I will put the chair on the slope and I will not forgive a survey out loud, even a true one. You can write the foot down as corrected. I will write nothing. When the next person with an instrument comes, they will find me uncomfortable and accurate. I suppose that is what you wanted. I wanted the chair.

n_mid_left.text: Then it stays, and I hate the speech where a foot of mercy is called a measurement. I am making it anyway. The map will be kind and false. Alma sits. The next kid with a better instrument will call her a thief unless somebody remembers we chose this. I am remembering it. I am not dressing it up.

n_end_left.text: Leave it. I will sit. I know the post is one foot inside my life and inside the line, and I am not confused about which of those I picked. You wanted me comfortable. I am comfortable and the map is wrong. If that eats at you, let it eat. I have the chair, which is the thing I asked for.

branches.summary: The Goshen post is moved one foot. Alma's dooryard is true and smaller, and she does not forgive it out loud.
The post stays one foot inside Alma's flat. The map remains kind and false, and the chair stays usable.
With Alma dead, Ned moves the post. The line is true, and he does not treat her absence as consent.
With Alma dead, Ned leaves the post. The kind, false foot remains because she asked for the chair.
With Ned dead, Alma moves the post herself. She keeps the chair's loss and does not forgive it out loud.
With Ned dead, Alma keeps the post and the chair. She states the false foot plainly and sits anyway.

rewards.detail: The Goshen corner is either corrected by one foot or left knowingly wrong so a chair can stay level.
Ellis chose between a true line that shrinks Alma's dooryard and a kind map that keeps her chair.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: The post stays, and Alma sets the chair on the flat and does not forgive a surveyor who never came. Ellis dies before the foot can be moved or defended. Ned has no speech to hate. The dooryard keeps its lie and its comfort.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The season ends with the post still one foot into the only level ground and nobody having chosen whether that foot is a theft or a mercy. Alma sits, but she sits in an argument that was never finished.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: Goshen has the foot decided. Either the post was moved and the chair went to the slope, or the post was left and the map stayed kindly false, and Alma knows which unforgiveness she is owed.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Alma is dead, so Ned stands in a dooryard whose chair he does not get to use as an excuse. He still hates both speeches. He can move the post now that comfort has left, or leave the false foot because she asked for the chair and the chair is empty.

n_open.text: Alma is dead. The chair is still on the only flat, and the post is still one foot into it. I hate the speech where we call that mercy and I hate the speech where we call the chair a crime. She isn't here to want the seat. You are here. Make one anyway. I will write what you make.

choices.text: Move the post now that Alma cannot sit in the argument.
Leave the false foot because Alma wanted the chair.

n_end_moved_ned.text: Moved. The line is true and the flat is smaller and the chair has nobody in it, which makes this feel cleaner than it is. She said she would not forgive it out loud. She can't. I won't pretend her silence is consent. I moved a post. The map matches the ground. That is the whole virtue, and it is small.

n_end_left_ned.text: It stays. She wanted the chair and the chair is empty and I am still leaving the lie because the request was about the flat, not about her pulse. The map is kind and false. I hate that sentence and it is the true one. The next instrument can call the dooryard a theft. They will be late.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Ned is dead, so Alma has no one to hate the speeches for her. She can still move the post or keep the chair, and she will say which wrongness she is willing to live beside without borrowing a surveyor's anger.

n_open.text: Ned is dead, so nobody is here to hate both sentences in advance. The post is one foot into my flat. I can have it moved and sit on the slope, or I can leave it and keep the chair and the false map. I know what I want. I am asking whether you will say the true part out loud with me.

choices.text: Move the post with Alma and give up the flat.
Leave the post and let Alma keep the level chair.

n_end_moved_alma.text: We moved it. I will sit badly and I will not forgive the foot out loud, even though I agreed to lose it. Agreement is not comfort. The line is true. Ned would have hated the speech and made it anyway. I made it without him. The chair goes to the slope tonight, before I can change into a liar.

n_end_left_alma.text: Then I sit. The map is wrong by a foot and I am comfortable, and I will say both halves when someone asks so they don't get to call me confused. Ned is not here to be angry at the paperwork. I can be plain without him. I would like the chair. I have it. The post stays in my life.

endingImplications: Alma Gray's dooryard is either made true, and her only flat chair goes to the slope, or left one foot wrong so she can sit in comfort. Ned has the speech he hated. The corner will not pretend the choice was neutral.

title: Fourteen Winters of Mail
summary: A box on the survey desk holds fourteen winters of unopened mail addressed to Ellis's successive bodies. Owen Perch will not inherit the office. He brought the box so Ellis would not feel clean. One letter can be opened, all of them can be opened, or the box can burn sealed.
discovery: The box is already on the desk in the rented room off Court Street, tape dull, fourteen winters of envelopes inside. Owen set it down and did not offer a key, because it was never locked. You are here because he is here. The mail is not somewhere else.

steps.playerAction: Look at the unopened box already on the survey desk and hear Owen say he did not bring it so you could feel clean.
Choose one letter, the whole box, or the stove, and do that choosing without sending anyone out for a missing envelope.
Leave the desk with either two sentences heard, the body-names said aloud, or the ash of mail that stayed sealed.

n_open.text: Fourteen winters. I counted the seasons, not the moral. The envelopes are addressed to the bodies in turn, and nobody opened them, and I will not inherit this office so don't offer me the habit. I brought the box so you would not feel clean. Open one, open all, or burn it sealed. The stove is in the corner.

choices.text: Open one letter and have it read aloud in the office.
Open the whole box and say the addressees aloud.
Burn the box in the office stove without opening it.

textVariants.text: You will want a second copy of whatever is in there, a clean page and a dirty one, so you can feel thorough. I didn't carry this upstairs for your thoroughness. The mail is to Rennet and Ada and the ones after, still shut. Say a name, read a page, or burn the pile. Don't make a duplicate of a silence and call it care.

n_mid_one.text: One. The envelope says Louis Pell and there is no return name, just a quarry hand that got tired of waiting at a rail. I am not opening a second to make you feel you were fair. You picked a single winter out of fourteen. I hope it sits badly. That was the point of bringing the box.

n_end_one.text: This is the letter, and I am saying it in my mouth so it cannot stay a relic. "Louis, Thursday's envelope is still fat because the pot is the job, and I will not pay the drill for a disagreement in your hands. Come take the cash before Sunday or I will write the week as unpaid, and I will not call that a punishment." That's the two sentences. The rest of the box stays shut, which is not cleanliness. It is a limit.

n_mid_all.text: All of them, then. I am cutting the tape and I am not sorting you a gentle order. Bills, a chair that was kept, a truck that was not yours, a spelling list, a compressor part. You wanted the pile. You don't get to feel clean at the bottom of it. I will say names before I say contents, because names are the part people skip.

n_end_all.text: I am saying them in this room. Rennet Moss. Ada Smollet. Those two first, out loud, before Louis Pell and Hannah Greer and Chris Dobbs and the one the certificate calls Rowan. Fourteen winters, six mouths the county thought were separate. You heard the names. The letters can be dull now. Dull is what you earned by opening them.

n_mid_burned.text: Sealed, then. The stove is lit and the box fits if I break the lid with my heel, which I am doing. You don't get a sentence from Louis or a name from Rennet. You also don't get to store the silence where it can make you feel careful. Ash is a decision. I want you to smell it so you don't call it abstract.

n_end_burned.text: It's burned unopened. Fourteen winters went up in a rented room and the desk is clear in the ugly way. I brought the box so you would not feel clean, and burning is one way to stay unclean and also one way to tidy. I hate that both are true. The stranger who wants this office later will not inherit the envelopes. That part I accept.

branches.summary: Owen opens one letter, to Louis Pell, and reads two sentences of it aloud. The rest of the fourteen winters stay sealed.
Owen opens every letter and says the addressees aloud, Rennet Moss and Ada Smollet first, then the bodies after them.
The box is burned sealed in the survey office stove. No letter is read, and Owen refuses to call the ash a cleaning.
With Owen dead, Willa reads the two sentences of the Louis Pell letter and leaves the rest sealed.
With Owen dead, Willa opens all the mail and names Rennet Moss and Ada Smollet aloud before the later bodies.
With Owen dead, Willa burns the sealed box and refuses to call the cleared desk a virtue.

rewards.detail: The survey desk either keeps one read letter, a fully opened box of body-mail, or the fact that the box was burned sealed.
Fourteen winters of mail were addressed to the successive bodies and had been left unopened on purpose.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Owen burns the box rather than leave it to a stranger. Ellis dies before choosing a letter. The stove takes fourteen winters sealed, and Owen does not read them to feel fair about the burning.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The box stays on the desk, tape intact, and the era turns. No letter is opened and no fire is lit. The next hands find fourteen winters of mail and the same temptation to feel clean.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The mail has been faced. Either one letter was read aloud, every addressee was named, or the sealed box was burned, and the office does not get to call the pile unfinished business.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Owen is dead, so Willa has the box he refused to turn into an inheritance. She believes a clean page is a weapon. She will still open one letter, open all, or burn the pile, and she will not let the office feel orderly about any of the three.

n_open.text: Owen is dead and the box is on the desk anyway. Fourteen winters, addressed to the bodies, still shut. He brought it so you would not feel clean, and I am not going to finish his refusal by filing it. Open one, open all, or burn it in that stove. A clean drawer is how this office stays unaccountable.

choices.text: Have Willa open one letter and read it aloud.
Have Willa open the box and name Rennet and Ada aloud.
Burn the sealed box and let Willa refuse to call it order.

n_end_one_willa.text: One envelope. Louis Pell. I am reading the only two sentences that matter and then I stop, because a sample is already a way of feeling prudent. "Louis, Thursday's envelope is still fat because the pot is the job, and I will not pay the drill for a disagreement in your hands. Come take the cash before Sunday or I will write the week as unpaid, and I will not call that a punishment." The rest stays shut. Prudence is not innocence.

n_end_all_willa.text: Rennet Moss. Ada Smollet. I said those two first, in this room, and then the later names, because a pile of bodies is not a texture. You have the letters open. If you make a fair copy of them you will sand off the grease. I will not help you sand. The names were the point Owen would have grudged you. Have them.

n_end_burned_willa.text: Burned, still sealed. The stove did the work and the desk looks managed, which I despise. Owen is dead so he doesn't get to hate it with me. I hate it enough. No stranger inherits the envelopes, and you don't inherit a quotation. If you wanted to feel careful, you failed. Good. Careful is too close to clean.

endingImplications: The unopened body-mail is either tasted in a single letter, spoken as a list of names beginning with Rennet and Ada, or burned sealed so no stranger inherits it. Owen does not become surveyor. Ellis does not get to feel clean.

title: The Slick Rock
summary: A stranger is on the slick rock at the Vergennes falls, and the coat-count is also Osier's job. He can climb or keep the numbers. He does not want a moral about water. He wants to know which job Ellis will shout.
discovery: You are already at the basin lip where the count sheet is weighted with a stone. The stranger is on the slick rock in plain sight, not hidden and not a rumor. Osier Rouleau has the tally in his hand and the climb in his legs, and he is waiting for a shout rather than a lesson.

steps.playerAction: See the stranger on the slick rock and the unfinished coat-count in Osier's hand at the same time.
Shout either for the stranger to come down, so Osier climbs, or for the count to continue, so nobody climbs.
Stay with the job you shouted until the stranger is on the gravel or the tally is finished without a rescue.

n_open.text: Stranger on the slick rock, and I am halfway through the coat-count. I can climb or I can keep the numbers. Both are my job and I cannot do them with the same hands. Don't tell me water has a moral. Tell me which job you are going to shout. I will do the one you shout.

choices.text: Shout the stranger down and send Osier onto the slick rock.
Shout the coat-count and do not send anyone onto the rock.

textVariants.text: You don't argue with where water wants a body, and you also can't stand a count left open. I am not interested in either of those as a sermon. The stranger is on the slick. The coats are half tallied. Shout the climb or shout the count. If you give me a proverb I will pretend the falls took it.

n_mid_pulled.text: The shout goes at the stranger, not at a moral, and Osier puts the count sheet under the stone and goes down the slick rock on his hands. The climb is the whole scene. He gets a grip on a wet sleeve, the stranger comes off the rock, and both of them hit the gravel coughing. Nobody produces a form. The count sheet stays where he left it.
