n_end_pulled.text: He's on the gravel. I climbed because you shouted that job and not the other. The coat-count is short and it will stay short until I am dry enough to care, which is not this minute. Don't thank the water. The water did not climb. I did, and you pointed. That is the division of the work.

n_mid_counted.text: Then I keep the numbers. You shouted the count, so I do not climb, and I do not ask the stranger to become a story while I am still missing three coats. The rock stays slick. The person stays on it. I am not going to look up between figures and call that looking a rescue. You picked the job. I am finishing it.

n_end_counted.text: The count is done and I did not climb. If the stranger comes down, they come down without my hands. If they don't, the falls keep them and the sheet does not. I wanted to know which job you would shout. You shouted this one. I will not add a sentence about water to make the sheet feel kinder than a sheet.

branches.summary: Ellis shouts the stranger down. Osier climbs the slick rock, pulls the stranger onto the gravel, and drops the coat-count.
Ellis shouts for the coat-count. Osier finishes the tally and does not climb, and the stranger is left on the slick rock.
With Osier dead, Marie sends a hand from the upper walk. The stranger is pulled off the slick rock and the count stays short.
With Osier dead, Marie finishes the coat-count and does not send anyone onto the slick rock.

rewards.detail: Ellis shouted either the climb or the coat-count, and Osier did that job rather than a sermon about the falls.
The slick rock and the coat-count were both Osier's work, and they could not be done with the same hands.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Osier climbs because Ellis's shout dies in the noise of the falls, and he cannot tell which job was meant. He goes down the slick rock anyway. The stranger comes off. The coat-count is short one, and there is no one left to say which shortage was chosen.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The stranger is still on the rock and the count is still open when the era turns. No shout settled the job. The basin keeps both the unfinished tally and the person on the slick.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The falls have a finished job. Either Osier climbed and the count went short, or the count was completed and the stranger was not pulled. The next body does not get to shout it over.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Osier is dead, so Marie holds the count sheet at the basin and will not pretend she is him. A hand from the upper walk can go down for the stranger, or the tally can be finished and the rock left alone. She still wants Ellis to shout one job, not a lesson.

n_open.text: Osier is dead and his sheet is in my hand. There is a stranger on the slick rock and the coat-count is unfinished. I will not pretend I am the man who climbs for a living. I can send a hand from the upper walk down, or I can finish the numbers and leave the rock. Which job are you shouting?

choices.text: Shout the stranger down and send the upper-walk hand.
Shout the count and leave the slick rock alone.

n_end_pulled_marie.text: I shouted your shout on, and the hand from the walk went down and brought the stranger onto the gravel. Osier is not here to be proud of the grip. The count is short. I will not pad the sheet to make a dead man's tally look finished. The person is off the rock. That is the job you picked.

n_end_counted_marie.text: Then I finish his numbers and I do not send anyone down. The stranger stays on the slick. I hate the looks I will get and I will not soften them with a speech about the falls. You shouted the count. Osier asked for a job, even if he is dead and I am the one holding the pencil. The sheet is complete. The rock is not my errand.

endingImplications: At the Vergennes falls, Osier either climbs the slick rock because Ellis shouted that job, leaving the coat-count short, or he finishes the count and does not climb. Water is not given a moral. The shout is the assignment.

title: Invoice the Mare
summary: Cora Belden promised the Morgan mare Invoice to a 4-H girl and also owes the feed man more than pride will cover. Ellis stands at the fence as witness, gets no share, and wears the blame of whichever way Cora goes. The choice is made here, not at the college farm.
discovery: Invoice is already in the paddock on Cora's side of the neighbor fence, and the feed bill is already in Cora's coat pocket. The girl is not in the scene. You are at the rail because Cora asked for a witness. The college farm's office is not where this is decided.

steps.playerAction: Stand at Cora Belden's fence, look at Invoice, and hear the promise and the feed bill as two real debts.
Witness either the mare going to the girl or the mare being sold against the bill, decided without leaving the rail.
Accept the blame of having stood there, and do not ask for a share of the horse or of the money.

n_open.text: Her name is Invoice. I promised her to the girl who did the 4-H work, and I owe the feed man more than my pride will cover. If you witness, you don't get a share. You get the blame of whichever way I go, because you stood at this fence. We are not walking over to the college farm to make it official. Official is a word they use for rooms I don't owe.

choices.text: Witness the promise: Invoice goes to the girl.
Witness the sale: Invoice goes against the feed bill.

textVariants.text: You will sign a thing just to end the standing-still, and the girl is a living promise while the feed man is paper. Invoice doesn't care which of those you find more serious. I need you to witness, not to flinch into a signature that makes you feel finished. The girl or the bill. The fence is the whole courthouse.

n_mid_girl.text: Then the girl gets her. I will tell the feed man the mare is not his collateral and he can hate me in arithmetic. You stood here, so when people say I was soft you are in the sentence. I am soft about a promise and hard about not hiding. The horse does not become a lesson. She becomes the girl's horse.

n_end_girl.text: Invoice goes to the girl. I will walk her as far as the girl's gate myself, later, not as a parade and not with you holding a rope for credit. You witnessed. The bill stays angry. I would rather an angry bill than a promise I broke at this fence and then blamed on a farm office I refused to enter.

n_mid_bill.text: Then I sell her against the bill, and I decide it here, not in an office with a brass plate. The feed man gets the money. The girl gets the truth from me, not from a rumor and not from you. You still get the blame of having stood at the rail while I said it. That was the wage of witnessing. There isn't another wage.

n_end_bill.text: She's sold against the feed bill. I will tell the girl myself, in a yard, without a speech about how mares teach character. I broke a promise because hay is not a mood. You watched me break it. If the county wants a villain it can use both our names. It does not get a share, and neither do you.

branches.summary: Invoice goes to the 4-H girl. Cora keeps the feed bill angry, and Ellis is the witness who gets the blame and no share.
Invoice is sold against the feed bill at the fence. Cora will tell the girl herself, and Ellis keeps only the blame.
With Cora dead, Ruth gives Invoice to the girl and tells the feed man himself that the bill stays unpaid by the mare.
With Cora dead, Ruth sells Invoice against the feed bill and tells the girl herself at the fence.

rewards.detail: Ellis witnessed Cora's choice and took the blame of the fence without taking a share of the mare.
Invoice was both a promise to a 4-H girl and a debt against the feed bill, and both were real at once.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Cora sells Invoice against the feed bill and tells the girl herself. Ellis dies before the witnessing can be shared, so the blame stays in Cora's mouth alone. She does not hide behind the college farm, and she does not send someone else to say the promise broke.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The mare is still in the paddock and both debts are still unpaid in the only way that matters. No one has witnessed a choice. The girl and the feed man are both still waiting on a sentence Cora has not said.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The fence has a result. Invoice either goes to the girl, with the bill left angry, or is sold against the bill, with the girl told by Cora. Ellis remains the witness of whichever one happened.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Cora is dead, so Ruth stands at the neighbor fence with a mare she did not promise and a bill she did not run up. She will not inherit Cora's silence. The girl can still have Invoice, or the feed man can be paid, and Ruth will say the loss out loud.

n_open.text: Cora is dead. I am not a horse woman and I am not walking this over to the college farm to be helped. Invoice is in the paddock. The girl was promised her. The feed man is owed more than pride. I can give the mare away or sell her against the bill. Pick the loss you will say out loud. I will say it with you.

choices.text: Give Invoice to the girl and let Ruth say the bill stays angry.
Sell Invoice against the bill and have Ruth face the girl.

n_end_girl_ruth.text: The girl gets the horse. I will tell the feed man the collateral died with the promise, not with Cora, and he can be angry at a living voice. I didn't make the promise. I am keeping it because breaking it in a dead woman's name would be a cheap kind of practical. You witnessed. Don't ask me for a share of anything with a mane.

n_end_bill_ruth.text: Sold. The feed man gets paid and I will tell the girl myself, because Cora said she would have, and I am not hiring a softer mouth. A promise lost to hay is still a loss. I am saying it at this fence. You stood here, so you are in the blame. You are not in the money. There is no money for you.

endingImplications: Invoice the mare either keeps Cora's promise to the 4-H girl or is sold at the fence against the feed bill. Ellis gets no share of the horse or the money, only the blame of having stood there. The college farm is not invited in.

title: A Renter for the East Room
summary: Ben Keene needs a winter room that is not the Cornwall attic. The east room is where the Quiet Household has kept the displaced. Renting it to a living neighbor is ordinary life. Refusing keeps a memorial. Eden can end the practice without mocking it. This is a key and a stove, not a last ceremony.
discovery: Ben is already in the east-room doorway with his coat on and no speech prepared. The bed is made because the house makes it, not because tonight is a rite. You are in Orwell because Eden asked the practical question out loud: a renter, or an empty room with a name in the drawer.

steps.playerAction: Stand in the east-room doorway and hear Ben ask for a winter that is not the Cornwall attic.
Choose whether a living neighbor rents the room or the household keeps it for the displaced.
Let Eden say the ending of the practice, or the keeping of it, without turning the key into a rite.

n_open.text: Ben needs a room with heat and a door that shuts. The Cornwall attic is damp and it isn't his. This room is where we kept the people the house would not let go. Renting it to him is ordinary life. Refusing him keeps a memorial. I can end a habit without making fun of my father. I am asking you which winter this bed is for.

choices.text: Rent the east room to Ben for the winter.
Keep the east room and refuse Ben the winter in it.

textVariants.text: You hate a gate left open, and an empty east room is a gate this house has refused to shut for years. Ben is a living neighbor with a cold attic waiting for him in Cornwall. If you keep the room, you are keeping a practice. If you rent it, you are finishing one. Eden will not mock either ending. She wants the latch decided.

n_mid_rented.text: Then I'll take it. I can pay a winter's rent and I can keep the stove fed, and I will not ask what the drawer was for unless the drawer is in my way. I don't have a voice for a choir and I don't want one. I want a door. If that insults the house, the house can be insulted by a living tenant. I've been insulted by damp longer.

n_end_rented.text: The room is rented. Ben gets the key and the heat, and the names don't get the bed. I am not going to mock the years we kept it empty. Father kept it because Mother asked. I am ending that because a neighbor needs a winter. Maren's certificate can stay in the kitchen drawer. It does not need a mattress to be true.

n_mid_kept.text: Then I don't get it. I'll say that plainly so you don't have to make it soft. The attic will still be the attic. I asked for a room, not for a meaning, and the answer is no. I can be embarrassed later. Right now I just need to know where I am sleeping, and it isn't here. Thank you for not dressing the no up as concern about my character.

n_end_kept.text: The room stays. Ben will find another winter and I will not pretend I saved him from something by refusing him. I kept a memorial because I am not ready to end it, and I am saying that without a joke. The bed remains for the displaced. A living neighbor was turned away. That is the cost, and it is ordinary and ugly, which is different from holy.

branches.summary: Eden rents the east room to Ben Keene. A living neighbor takes the bed, and the household practice loses the room without being mocked.
Eden keeps the east room. Ben is refused a winter there, and the refusal is named as a memorial rather than as concern.
With Eden dead, Joel rents the east room to Ben. The practice ends without Joel using the moment to mock it.
With Eden dead, Joel keeps the east room. Ben is refused, and Joel does not pretend the refusal is modern or funny.
With Ben dead, Eden rents the east room to another living neighbor. The practice ends as housing, not as a substitute rite.
With Ben dead, Eden still keeps the east room. She refuses a living renter and does not call the emptiness holy.

rewards.detail: The east room is either Ben's rented winter or still closed to living neighbors.
Eden either ended the empty-room practice without mocking it or kept the memorial and said so plainly.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Eden refuses the renter because a dead Ellis cannot be asked twice. Ben does not get the east room. She would rather keep a memorial than invent a consent the body can no longer give, and she does not mock the habit she is unwilling to end alone.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The winter arrives with the east room still empty and Ben still in the Cornwall attic. Nobody has rented the bed and nobody has defended the emptiness. The practical question stays practical and unanswered.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The east room has a winter assigned. Either Ben rents it as a living neighbor, or the household keeps it and says the keeping is a memorial. The plates are not the subject. The key is.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Eden is dead, so Joel has to answer Ben about the room he grew up resenting. He can rent it without making his daughter's ending into a joke, or he can keep it because she is not here to finish the practice for him.

n_open.text: Eden is dead and Ben still needs a winter that isn't a damp attic in Cornwall. This is the east room. I kept it because my mother asked, which is not the same as believing it feeds anyone. I can rent it to him or I can refuse. I will not mock Eden's question by turning it into one of my old complaints.

choices.text: Have Joel rent the east room to Ben.
Have Joel keep the room and send Ben back to the attic.

n_end_rented_joel.text: Joel gave me the key. I'll pay the winter and I'll keep my questions out of the drawers. Eden isn't here to say the ending, so I won't say it for her. I have a door that shuts. That was the ask. If the house feels thinner because a living person is in the bed, the house can feel thinner. I was cold.

n_end_kept_joel.text: I'm keeping it. Eden might have ended this and I won't end it over her absence just to feel modern. Ben doesn't get the winter. I am sorry about the attic and I am not going to pretend sorry is a stove. The room stays for the names. That may be stubborn. It is not a joke. I know the difference. I grew up in it.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Ben is dead, so the particular renter is gone and the practical question is not. Eden can still rent the east room to a living neighbor or keep it, and she will not use Ben's death as a reason to sneer at either choice.

n_open.text: Ben is dead. The attic question came with him and a neighbor who works the plow shed asked this morning for the same winter, ordinary as a key. I can rent the east room to a living person or I can keep it. I will not mock the old practice, and I will not pretend Ben can be asked again. The bed is still a bed.

choices.text: Rent the room to the living neighbor anyway.
Keep the east room empty even with Ben gone.

n_end_rented_eden.text: Then the plow-shed neighbor gets the key. Ben doesn't, because Ben can't. I am not replacing him with a symbol. I am heating a room. The names can live in the kitchen drawer without a mattress. Father kept this because he was asked. I am renting it because a living person was cold. That is the whole theology I am willing to have today.

n_end_kept_eden.text: I am keeping it. The neighbor can be disappointed in an ordinary way. I am not ready to end the room just because the first person who asked is dead. A memorial that collapses at the first absence was only waiting for an excuse. I don't have the excuse. The bed stays made. I won't call that holy. I'll call it not finished.

endingImplications: The Orwell east room is either rented to Ben Keene for an ordinary winter, which ends the practice of keeping it for the displaced, or refused, which leaves the memorial in place. Eden does not turn the choice into a ceremony and does not sneer at the years before it.

title: Thursday or Wednesday
summary: Gina has Vito's drill log at the overhang. The paper says a man drilled on Thursday. The chalk says he was buried on Wednesday. Marc will not average those into a Friday. Ellis has to treat one of them as true and leave the other as a disagreement, not a blend.
discovery: The log and the chalked note are already on the stone at the cut, and the jar for disagreements is already beside them. You are under the overhang because Gina and Marc are under it. Vito is not coming up to pick a column. The two days are the whole problem.

steps.playerAction: Read the drill log and the chalk where they already sit on the stone, Thursday against Wednesday.
Choose which day is treated as true, and refuse any blend that would invent a Friday for the sake of the pen.
Leave the losing day in the jar as a disagreement Marc is willing to hate and unwilling to average.

n_open.text: Vito's log is on the stone. He is not coming up the cut to defend a column, so don't leave a silence for him to fill. The paper says the man drilled Thursday. The chalk says that man was buried Wednesday. Marc will not sand those into a Friday. You pick which one we treat as true. The other one goes in the jar as a disagreement.

choices.text: Treat the chalk as true: he was buried Wednesday.
Treat the paper as true: he drilled on Thursday.

textVariants.text: You want both pages kept so you never have to stand on one. Marc's hand won't do that for you. Thursday is in the log. Wednesday is in the chalk. A second copy is not a third day. If the record is going to hold, it has to hold a single day, and the jar can hold the loser without pretending they agreed.

n_mid_chalk.text: Wednesday, then. I will not make the paper say a prettier neighbor to the chalk. If he was buried Wednesday he did not drill Thursday, and the log is wrong, and wrong can be written down as wrong. My hand hates a blank and it hates a blend more. Gina, the chalk wins. I am not averaging my pen into a Friday to keep the peace.

n_end_chalk.text: Chalk wins. The man was buried Wednesday, and Thursday's drilling is a lie we are willing to store. The paper goes in the jar beside the note so nobody later says we lost it. We didn't lose it. We demoted it. Hannah, if your bookkeeper's mouth wants a balanced column, it doesn't get one. Disagreement is the balance.

n_mid_paper.text: Thursday, then. The log is the record I am willing to be hated for, and the chalk is what somebody needed to write when the week went bad. I will not scratch the chalk off. I will not add a Friday so the two can shake hands. Paper wins. The chalk remains as the disagreement it is. My handwriting is not a peace treaty.

n_end_paper.text: Paper wins. He drilled Thursday, and the burial-chalk is in the jar with the log's copy so the losing day is not scrubbed into good manners. I have more names in that jar than any stone will take. This one is a day, not a man we invented. Marc can stand it. I can stand it. A Friday would have been the part I could not.

branches.summary: The chalk is treated as true. The man was buried Wednesday, and the Thursday drilling stays in the jar as a lie they are keeping.
The drill log is treated as true. Thursday stands, and the Wednesday chalk is kept in the jar as disagreement rather than erased.
With Gina dead, the chalk still wins. Paulette jars the Thursday paper and Marc refuses to invent a Friday.
With Gina dead, the paper wins. Paulette keeps Wednesday in the jar as a missing day and does not soften it.
With Marc dead, Gina lets the chalk win and jars Thursday. She keeps his refusal to average without inventing a new day.
With Marc dead, Gina lets the paper win. Wednesday goes in the jar, and she does not invent a Friday to close the week.

rewards.detail: The cut keeps one day as the true day, Thursday or Wednesday, and stores the other in the jar unblended.
Vito's paper and the chalk named different days, and a Friday would have been an invention rather than a record.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Both the log and the chalk stay in the jar, and nobody averages them into a Friday. Ellis dies before the pick. Gina lids the disagreement. Marc puts the pen down rather than invent a day that would make his hand feel finished.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The overhang keeps two days and no decision. Thursday and Wednesday remain side by side, and the next season inherits the temptation to sand them into something a payroll could love.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: One day was treated as true and the other was jarred as a disagreement. The cut does not carry a blended Friday forward. Marc's refusal to average stands with whichever day won.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Gina is dead, so Paulette has the jar and will not write a blank day to make the selectboard feel tended. Marc still refuses a Friday. Between them the chalk or the paper can win, and the missing day stays missing.

n_open.text: Gina is dead and I kept the jar. I didn't keep a job writing softness. The paper says Thursday. The chalk says Wednesday. Marc will not average them and neither will I. Pick the day you will stand next to. The other day stays missing on purpose. Missing is a truth. Don't ask me to sand it.

choices.text: Let the chalk win and have Paulette jar the paper.
Let the paper win and keep the chalk as the missing day.

n_end_chalk_paulette.text: Wednesday. I wrote that the log is the disagreement, not the day. Paulette didn't ask me to make it beautiful and I didn't. Gina is dead so she doesn't get a vote from the chalk she kept. The chalk still wins because you said so. A Friday is not hiding in my pen. I checked.

n_end_paper_paulette.text: Thursday stands. The chalk goes in the jar as the day we are willing to call wrong, and I am not rewriting it into a gentler week. If a name is missing, the missing is the truth. Here a day is missing. Marc can live with his hand. I can live with the stone not getting a softened list. You picked. That's the record.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Marc is dead, so his refusal to average has to be kept by someone else's mouth. Gina will not invent the Friday he hated just because the pen is free. The chalk or the paper still has to win, and the jar still takes the loser.

n_open.text: Marc is dead. I will not average his refusal into a Friday just because nobody is here to hate my handwriting. The log says the man drilled Thursday. The chalk says he was buried Wednesday. I can treat the chalk as true or the paper as true. I cannot treat them as neighbors. You pick the day. I will put the other in the jar.

choices.text: Treat Wednesday's chalk as the true day.
Treat Thursday's paper as the true day.

n_end_chalk_gina.text: Chalk. He was buried Wednesday and the Thursday line is a mistake I am keeping in glass so we don't get praised for losing it. Marc would have refused the blend. I am refusing it without him. The cut can live with one true day. It has lived with worse disagreements, and none of them became kinder by being averaged.

n_end_paper_gina.text: Paper. He drilled Thursday, and the chalk is the disagreement, not the correction. I am saying that in the cut where Marc's hand isn't. The jar gets Wednesday. I don't feel clean. A single day is not cleanliness. It is a refusal to invent Friday for the comfort of a closed week. That was his standard. It can be mine for this stone.

endingImplications: At the Bristol cut, either the chalk is true and the man was buried Wednesday, or the drill log is true and he worked Thursday. The losing day stays in the jar. No one invents a Friday to spare the pen.

title: The Letter Sylvia Hid
summary: Sylvia kept one letter out of the unsent sack because the envelope says Bram Voss, and she is a coward with good pitch. The letter can go into Cal's hand to hold, whether Bram is living or not. It can be read aloud in the loft, where he cannot answer. Or it can stay unopened.
discovery: The envelope is already on the loft stove's cool edge, addressed to Bram and kept out of the sack on purpose. Cal is in the room because Sylvia finally could not keep the address to herself. You are above the Cornwall grange. Nobody has to carry the letter to a landing for the choice to count.

steps.playerAction: Look at the envelope Sylvia held out of the sack and hear that the name on it is Bram Voss.
Choose whether Cal holds it for Bram, whether it is read in the loft where Bram cannot answer, or whether it stays sealed.
Leave the letter in a hand, in the air of the loft, or back in hiding, without taking it on a road.

n_open.text: This one was never in the sack. I kept it out because the outside says Bram Voss, and the name might still be a living man, and I am a coward with good pitch. I can hear a true note and I still hid the paper. Cal is here. You can put it in his hand to hold, you can make me read it where Bram cannot answer, or you can let me keep it shut.

choices.text: Put the sealed letter in Cal's hand to hold for Bram.
Have Sylvia read the letter aloud in the loft.
Keep the letter unopened and do not put it in Cal's hand.

textVariants.text: You cannot stand a letter left half-decided, and you want Bram's name said rather than stored. Sylvia's pitch is good and her nerve is not. The envelope is already out. If you make her finish it, finish it in this loft. Cal can hold it. The air can hear it. The sack does not get to become a road.

n_mid_held.text: I'll hold it. I will not promise you he is alive and I will not promise you he isn't. My hand is not a delivery and it is not a burial. If Bram can take it, he can take it from me. If he cannot, I still have the envelope and I have not invented a death to make the holding feel finished. Sylvia, you can stop clutching the air.

n_end_held.text: Then it leaves my loft in a living hand that knows his name. That is as brave as I am today, which is not very, and it is more than hiding. Cal has it sealed. Bram may be somewhere to receive it or he may not. I am not going to sing a guess. The pitch I trust is the one that says the letter is no longer only mine.

n_mid_read.text: If you read it, read it here. I am not taking you to a stone and I am not taking you to a landing to make the paper feel more serious. Bram is not in this loft. He cannot answer. I can stand that. I would rather hear the sentences than watch Sylvia decide they are too delicate for a room with a stove in it.

n_end_read.text: Then I open it, and these are the two sentences, and I will not add a harmony. "Bram, the ice will sound like it is talking, and I want you to stay off it anyway, even when I have told the landing the opposite. Take the pencil out of the drawer and mark what you can stand on, and do not wait for me to become a careful man." He is not here to answer. The loft heard it. That is as far as the letter goes.

n_mid_kept.text: Then it stays mine and it stays shut. I am a coward with the address showing, which is a poor kind of courage. Cal has seen the name and not the sentences. I will not call that a kindness to Bram. I will call it fear of a true note I already recognized. The sack does not get this one back. Neither does the road.

n_end_kept.text: You didn't tell me the sentence. I can live with not knowing what the ice-line said. I cannot live with you calling the hiding a protection if it was only your nerve failing. I know the letter exists. I don't have it. Bram, living or not, doesn't have it either. That is the choice. I will not steal it off the stove to improve you.

branches.summary: Sylvia puts the sealed letter in Cal's hand to hold for Bram, living or not. The loft does not invent which of those he is.
Sylvia reads two sentences of the letter aloud in the loft, where Bram cannot answer. The letter is not carried to a stone or a landing.
The letter stays unopened in the loft. Cal knows it exists and is not given the sentences or the envelope.
With Sylvia dead, Walter gives Cal the sealed letter to hold for Bram and says the rest of the rule still stands.
With Sylvia dead, Walter reads the two sentences in the loft. Bram cannot answer, and Walter does not call the reading a rule.
With Sylvia dead, the letter stays sealed. Walter keeps the rule, and Cal knows the name without the sentences.
With Cal dead, Ida holds the sealed letter for Bram. Sylvia lets it go without pretending Ida is a substitute son.
With Cal dead, Sylvia reads the two sentences in the loft. Ida hears them and Bram still cannot answer.
With Cal dead, Sylvia keeps the letter sealed. Ida names the fear as ordinary and does not take the envelope.

rewards.detail: The letter to Bram is either in Cal's keeping, read into the loft, or still sealed in Sylvia's hiding.
Ellis made Sylvia finish, hand off, or keep the cowardice she already named, without sending the letter on a road.

deathTransition.ifEllisDiesMidQuest: Sylvia re-hides the letter and Cal is not told. Ellis dies before the envelope can be put in a hand or read aloud. The address stays Bram's, the sentences stay shut, and the loft goes back to looking like a sack and a stove and nothing withheld.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfUnresolved: The letter remains on the edge of the decision, neither held nor read nor frankly kept. Sylvia's courage stays unfinished, and Cal leaves knowing only that she was afraid of a name.
deathTransition.onEraAdvanceIfResolved: The hidden letter has a fate. Cal holds it for Bram, the loft has heard two sentences Bram cannot answer, or Sylvia keeps it sealed with Cal as witness to the withholding. The sack is not pretended to be the whole truth.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Sylvia is dead, so Walter has the letter she excepted from her own rule. He is afraid of ad-hoc mercy and will say so. Cal can still hold it, hear it, or watch it stay sealed. Walter will not pretend a feeling is a stamp.

n_open.text: Sylvia is dead. This letter was never in the sack because the outside says Bram Voss and she was afraid of a living name. I don't like ad-hoc mercy. Undeliverable is a rule, and this envelope is a temptation to break it kindly. Cal is here. Hold it, read it in this loft, or leave it shut. I will hate the kindness and still do the one you pick.

choices.text: Have Walter put the sealed letter in Cal's hand.
Have the letter read in the loft with Sylvia gone.
Leave the letter sealed and let Walter keep the rule.

n_end_held_walter.text: Walter gave it over like a man handing me a problem with the corners squared. I'll hold it for Bram. I am not announcing whether my brother can receive mail. Walter can keep his rule for the rest of the sack. This one is in my hand because Sylvia died still hiding it, and hiding is not the same as a regulation.

n_end_read_walter.text: I read it, and I hate that reading feels like a kindness I didn't earn. Two sentences, then I stop. "Bram, the ice will sound like it is talking, and I want you to stay off it anyway, even when I have told the landing the opposite. Take the pencil out of the drawer and mark what you can stand on, and do not wait for me to become a careful man." He is not in this loft to answer. The rule survived everything except this page.

n_end_kept_walter.text: Then it stays shut and I still know the name. Walter is relieved in a way he is trying not to enjoy. I won't steal it. Sylvia is dead and the cowardice outlived her, which is a miserable inheritance and an honest one. Bram gets nothing today. The loft gets a rule instead of a sentence. I can hate that without correcting it.

ifNpcDead.resolution: Cal is dead, so Ida stands in the loft with Sylvia and will not let the letter become a song about a son. She can hold it for Bram, hear it read, or watch Sylvia keep it, and she will feed the decision with names rather than with comfort.

n_open.text: Cal is dead. I am not putting a bowl where he stood and calling that an answer. Sylvia kept a letter out because it says Bram. I can hold it for him, living or not. I can hear it read in this loft. Or I can watch her hide it again. Names are ingredients. Don't serve me a sauce. Serve me the paper's fate.

choices.text: Put the sealed letter in Ida's hand to hold for Bram.
Read the two sentences in the loft for Ida to hear.
Keep the letter sealed even with Ida in the room.

n_end_held_ida.text: Ida has it, sealed, and she will not pretend she is Cal. Bram's name is in a living hand that fed him and will not invent whether he can still take a letter. I am still a coward. I am a coward who let go. The pitch of that is not pretty. It is accurate, which is the note I was afraid of hitting.

n_end_read_ida.text: Ida wanted the paper's fate, so here it is in the air. "Bram, the ice will sound like it is talking, and I want you to stay off it anyway, even when I have told the landing the opposite. Take the pencil out of the drawer and mark what you can stand on, and do not wait for me to become a careful man." He cannot answer from this loft. I will not hum after it. The sentences are enough ingredient.

n_end_kept_ida.text: Then keep it, and don't ask me to call the keeping a meal. I know the name and not the inside. Cal is dead so he can't be disappointed for me. I am disappointed on my own account. Bram, wherever he is, is not fed by a hidden envelope. Sylvia's pitch is good. Her nerve is ordinary. Ordinary fear can stay in the loft. I won't steal it to improve her.

endingImplications: The letter Sylvia hid from the unsent sack either rests in Cal's hand for Bram, living or not, or is read in the Cornwall loft where he cannot answer, or stays sealed because her nerve fails in front of a witness. No one carries it off to settle the question by travel.
